effect_estimate.comment: Cross-sectional OLS regressions test whether local income inequality and democratic local government ownership (vs. state PUC-regulated investor ownership) predict progressive residential water tariff design. Positive inequality associations remain statistically significant across UPRs from 12,000 to 60,000 gallons/month (Figure 4). Subsample analyses noted in Endnote 17 indicate the inequality-progressivity relationship holds only for public utilities, though the interaction term in pooled Model B is not statistically significant.
effect_estimate.value: In OLS regressions of residential water rate progressivity (Unit Price Ratio [UPR] of average price/gal at 30,000 gal/month vs. 6,000 gal/month; N = 1,183 utilities, R^2 = 0.062), service-area income inequality (mean-to-median income ratio) correlates positively with rate progressivity in Model A (b = 0.310, p = 0.005; +0.08 SD in UPR per 1 SD increase in inequality), while private investor ownership correlates negatively with progressivity (b = -0.167, p = 0.000). In interaction Model B (N = 1,183, R^2 = 0.062), inequality correlates positively with UPR among local government utilities (b = 0.332, p = 0.005), whereas the Private x Inequality interaction is negative but not statistically significant (b = -0.209, p = 0.387; Private main effect b = 0.098, p = 0.749). Log population (b = 0.068, p = 0.014 in Model A) and log median income (b = 0.196, p = 0.000 in Model A) also correlate positively with rate progressivity.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Observational cross-sectional OLS design (capped below 3); primary empirical analysis documents a statistical association between local income inequality, public vs. PUC-regulated private utility governance, and progressive tariff structures without directly observing rate-making deliberations or household-level billing impacts (six municipal/utility examples are cited only from secondary sources).

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines residential water rate structures and fixed/volumetric user charges (fees) as redistributive policy, comparing locally elected municipal/county/special-district rate-setting accountable to voters with public input against state Public Utilities Commission (PUC) rate-setting for investor-owned utilities (participation).

outcome_flags.comment: Evaluates residential water tariff progressivity (Unit Price Ratio comparing unit prices at high discretionary consumption volumes against a 6,000 gallons/month basic indoor household water affordability benchmark). Sewer/sanitation rates are explicitly excluded (Endnote 5).

sample_size.value: 1,189 community water utilities serving >=40,000 residents (1,055 local government-owned and 134 investor-owned utilities, serving 183,314,934 residents total); N = 1,183 utilities in descriptive statistics and OLS regression models

study_design.comment: Authors cross-sectionally analyze single-family residential water rate schedules collected in early 2019 across US community water systems serving >=40,000 people using OLS regressions with robust standard errors, explicitly noting the cross-sectional nature of the data in the limitations section.
study_design.value: Quantitative cross-sectional observational study using multivariable ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with robust standard errors
